title: Classical Education Is Participation in a Wonderful Conversation
author: Andrew M. Selby
summary: Andrew Selby, writing for the Humanitas Institute, presents classical Christian education as an invitation into the Great Conversation, Mortimer Adler's phrase for the history of ideas. He begins with the childhood memory of being allowed to sit at the adults' table and wanting to take part in talk that obviously mattered. He argues that classical schools teach the rules of good conversation: seeking to understand before being understood, crafting arguments that are both true and persuasive, and being authentic. He connects this to the Christian idea of discipleship as lifelong learning within one body, and credits parents and a great books program for modeling the dialectic for him. His conclusion is that students must be formed as people who can enjoy conversations that shape churches, communities and the world, and that this is why he has built a career in classical Christian education.
points: Selby defines conversation as the free trading of ideas in a community, and argues that this exchange forms the beliefs on which lives are built.
Classical education is framed as formation in the habits of dialogue, including listening to understand, arguing both truthfully and persuasively, and refusing to project a false image.
Adler's "Great Conversation" casts reading the great books as joining a living discussion with those who came before, not consuming a canon.
The Christian notion of discipleship as lifelong learning in one body supplies a theological reason to value conversation.
Deep conversation both is substantial and moves somewhere, which separates it from small talk and from stalemated family arguments.
quotes: Classical education loves conversation. It seeks to build communities of people who can think well together.

In our classrooms, students learn the rules for engagement: to seek to understand someone else and not just be understood, to craft arguments that are both true and persuasive, to be authentic and not project images of what we would like to be.

Conversation can be defined as the free trading of ideas in a community. This swapping of ideas shapes who we are and what we do, since it often forms the beliefs that become the foundation for our lives.
We are invited into the lively, ongoing discussion with those who have gone before us as well as those we can speak to now.

If we want our students to join in conversations that really matter—the ones that will shape our churches, communities, and the world—then we have to teach them to be the kinds of people who can enjoy great conversations.

While some conversations can be insubstantial but move effectively, like chatting with the neighbor about the weather, others can be substantial but not get anywhere, like so many Thanksgiving dinner conversations with families divided over politics.
Our schools teach young people to grow into adults who want conversations that matter.
